title: “Behold, I Am Doing a New Thing”
paragraphs:
“Behold, I Am Doing a New Thing”
The Deeper Meaning of Isaiah 43:19 and the God Who Rewrites Broken Stories
There are moments in life when the weight of yesterday feels heavier than the hope of tomorrow.
Some people carry the memory of betrayal.
Others carry the shame of addiction.
Some silently replay the worst decision they ever made.
Others wake up every morning wondering if God can still use someone like them.
The hardest prison is often not made of steel.
It is made of memories.
It is built from regret.
And many people who love Jesus still live there.
That is why Isaiah 43:19 is one of the most powerful declarations in all of Scripture.
Not because it promises a better future.
But because it reveals the heart of a God who specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
The verse says:

“Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.”
— Isaiah 43:19 (ESV)
The original Hebrew begins with a word loaded with urgency:
הִנְנִי (hinneni)
It means:

“Look.”
“Pay attention.”
“Behold.”
“Do not miss this.”
God is essentially saying:
“Stop everything and watch what I am about to do.”
This is not merely encouragement.
This is divine interruption.
God is confronting people who have become trapped by their past.
The context matters.
Isaiah was speaking to Israel, a nation that had repeatedly failed God.
They had rebelled.
Ignored His commands.
Chased idols.
Broken covenant after covenant.
If anyone deserved rejection, it was them.
Yet instead of announcing destruction, God announces renewal.
That alone should stop every believer in their tracks.
Because the Gospel has always been about scandalous grace.
The God who had every right to walk away instead moved closer.
The God who could have abandoned His people instead declared:
“I am doing a new thing.”
Notice what He says just before Isaiah 43:19.
In Isaiah 43:18 He says:
“Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old.”
This does not mean God wants His people to forget history.
The Bible constantly remembers history.
Rather, God is warning them not to become so obsessed with what He did yesterday that they fail to see what He is doing today.
Many believers celebrate the Red Sea while missing the river God is creating in the desert right now.
Some people are so focused on old wounds that they cannot recognize new healing.
Others are so focused on old failures that they cannot recognize new mercy.
Still others are so focused on old victories that they cannot recognize new assignments.
God is bigger than your last chapter.
The phrase:
חֲדָשָׁה (chadashah)
translated as “new thing,” does not merely mean recent.
It carries the idea of something fresh, renewed, extraordinary, and unprecedented.
God is not simply improving the old.
He is creating something that did not exist before.
This theme echoes throughout Scripture.
When Jesus arrives, He does not merely repair humanity.
He transforms it.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:
καινός (kainos)
meaning “new in quality.”
Not merely newer in time.
Different.
Transformed.
Made new at the deepest level.
Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 5:17
The Greek says:
καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis)
“A completely new creation.”
Not a repaired version.
Not a cleaned-up version.
A new creation.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to improve sinners.
He came to redeem them.
To transform them.
To rewrite them.
To make dead things live again.
That is why Isaiah 43:19 ultimately points beyond Israel's immediate restoration.
It points toward Christ.
Because every road in Scripture eventually leads to Jesus.
The wilderness in Isaiah is not merely geographic.
It is spiritual.
The desert is not merely sand.
It is the human heart without God.
The wilderness is where hope dries up.
Where prayers feel unanswered.
Where dreams seem buried.
Where people wonder if they have gone too far to be forgiven.
Yet God says:
“I will make a way.”
The Hebrew word is:
דֶּרֶךְ (derekh)
A road.
A path.
A journey.
A route where none existed.
Centuries later Jesus would stand before humanity and declare:

“I am the way.”
— John 14:6
The Greek:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδός (egō eimi hē hodos)
“I am the way.”
Isaiah says God will make a way.
Jesus says He is the way.
The connection is impossible to miss.
The road in the wilderness has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You are not defined by your worst moment.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery and murder.
Rahab was a prostitute.
Moses was a fugitive.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet God rewrote every one of their stories.
The Bible is not a collection of perfect people.
It is a testimony of what happens when imperfect people encounter a perfect Savior.
That is why our theme remains so powerful:
Because that is the story of Scripture.
And if we are honest, it is our story too.
Some readers carry hidden scandals no one knows about.
Some carry secret addictions.
Some carry private regrets.
Some smile publicly while grieving privately.
Some have convinced themselves that God can forgive everyone except them.
But Isaiah 43:19 destroys that lie.
God does not specialize in finding worthy people.
He specializes in transforming broken people.
He takes deserts and creates rivers.
He takes graves and creates testimonies.
He takes scandals and turns them into stories of grace.
The greatest evidence of this is the Cross.
At Calvary, humanity committed its worst crime.
The sinless Son of God was crucified.
What looked like history's greatest defeat became history's greatest victory.
The resurrection proved that God is able to write endings no human being could imagine.
And He is still doing it.
Right now.
In lives all over the world.
Perhaps even in yours.
Maybe your marriage feels like a desert.
Maybe your faith feels exhausted.
Maybe your heart feels numb.
Maybe your future feels uncertain.
Maybe you cannot see the river yet.
But rivers often begin underground before they become visible.
God is often working before we recognize His work.
That is why Isaiah asks:
“Do you not perceive it?”
The problem is not always God's activity.
Sometimes it is our inability to recognize it.
Faith learns to trust God's hand before it sees the evidence.
The same God who opened the Red Sea.
The same God who raised Lazarus.
The same God who rolled away the stone.
The same God who redeemed Peter.
The same God who transformed Paul.
The same God who conquered death through Jesus Christ is still writing stories today.
Your story is not finished.
The chapter you are living in is not the conclusion.
The Author is still writing.
And when Jesus holds the pen, grace always has the final word.
If this message stirred something in your spirit, do not keep it to yourself.
What wilderness has God brought you through?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because every share spreads the Gospel.
Every comment strengthens community.
Every saved article preserves biblical encouragement.
And every transformed life glorifies Jesus Christ.
The wilderness is not your final destination.
The river is already on its way.
The God who wrote redemption into history is still writing redemption into your story.
